coverage: All eight Books in both English editions. A systematic treatise, not a dialogue -- per editorial policy's guidance for treatises, almost every entry is Reference. Two entries are Major for sustained, argued-with engagement across multiple Books: Socrates and Plato, the target of most of Book 2. Nine genuine namesake collisions (Dionysius, Periander, Thrasybulus, Pausanias x3, Cleisthenes, Timophanes, plus the clean epithet-resolved splits Amyntas/Chares/Pheidon) are resolved in build_aristotle_politics.py and documented in README.md, alongside a serious source defect: original-en's Gutenberg/Bekker-apparatus text bleeds editorial footnotes and page headers into the running prose at many points, accounting for the two "Aristotle" self-citations excluded as apparatus and the one entity (Sardanapalus) present in modern-en only.

entities.name: Socrates
entities.body: As the speaker in Plato's Republic and Laws, the source of the community-of-women-and-property proposals that occupy most of Book 2's opening critique, and of the cyclical theory of constitutional change Aristotle rebuts at the close of Book 5.

entities.name: Plato
entities.body: Author of the Republic and the Laws, whose proposed constitutions are examined at length in Book 2 and revisited in Books 4 and 7; cited by name as the author distinct from his speaker Socrates.

entities.name: Hesiod
entities.body: The early Greek poet, quoted for the line "First house and wife and an ox for the plough."

entities.name: Charondas
entities.body: The lawgiver of Catana, cited in Book 1 for a term he used for household members and, in Book 2, for the laws he gave his own and other Chalcidian cities in Italy and Sicily.

entities.name: Epimenides the Cretan
entities.body: Cited for a term he used for household members, alongside Charondas.

entities.name: Homer
entities.body: The poet, quoted repeatedly (Books 1, 3, 4) -- on the Cyclopes' households, on the "tribeless, lawless, hearthless" man outside the state, and on Agamemnon's power over Achilles.

entities.name: Solon
entities.body: The Athenian lawgiver, quoted in Book 1 on the limitlessness of wealth, and credited in Book 2 with laws against unlimited land ownership and with reshaping the Athenian constitution by opening the law courts to all citizens.

entities.name: Midas
entities.body: The legendary king whose golden touch is cited as an example of wealth that cannot feed a man.

entities.name: Theodectes
entities.body: The tragedian whose play Helen is quoted for a line about noble birth.

entities.name: Daedalus
entities.body: The legendary craftsman, whose self-moving statues are cited as an image of tools needing no servants to operate them.

entities.name: Hephaestus
entities.body: The god of craftsmanship, whose self-moving tripods are cited alongside the statues of Daedalus as an image of tools needing no servants.

entities.name: Amasis
entities.body: The Egyptian king, whose saying about his footpan is cited as an example of ceremony distinguishing a ruler from his subjects.

entities.name: Gorgias
entities.body: The rhetorician, cited in Book 1 for enumerating the virtues, and again in Book 3 (as "Gorgias of Leontini") for his ironic remark that citizens, like kettles, are manufactured by magistrates.

entities.name: Chares of Paros
entities.body: One of the writers on tillage and planting Aristotle cites. A different, unrelated "Chares" -- a political intermediary, not this agricultural writer -- appears later, in Book 5.

entities.name: Apollodorus of Lemnos
entities.body: One of the writers on tillage and planting Aristotle cites, alongside Chares of Paros.

entities.name: Thales
entities.body: The philosopher, cited for his olive-press monopoly, told as an anecdote about how philosophers could be rich if they chose. Book 2 also reports (and calls chronologically inconsistent) a tradition making a "Thales" the teacher of Lycurgus and Zaleucus -- most likely the same figure invoked by a strained legendary genealogy rather than a second, unnamed person.

entities.name: Cleisthenes of Athens
entities.body: The Athenian reformer who, after the expulsion of the tyrants, enrolled strangers, slaves, and resident aliens into new tribes (3:5) and later strengthened the democracy by similar measures (6:11). A different, unrelated Cleisthenes -- his maternal grandfather, the tyrant of Sicyon -- appears in Book 5.

entities.name: Pheidon the Corinthian
entities.body: An ancient legislator credited with the view that the number of citizen families should remain fixed. A different, unrelated Pheidon -- a king of Argos who became a tyrant -- appears in Book 5.

entities.name: Hippodamus
entities.body: The son of Euryphon, of Miletus: inventor of the grid-plan city and layout of the Piraeus, and the first non-statesman to write on the ideal constitution -- his own three-class model occupies most of Book 2's discussion of him.

entities.name: Lycurgus
entities.body: The traditional lawgiver of Sparta, credited with its constitution and common meals, said to have studied the Cretan constitution during King Charilaus's minority.

entities.name: Charilaus
entities.body: The Spartan king whose minority Lycurgus is said to have guarded before traveling to Crete (2:53). A later reference to "the tyranny of Charilaus at Lacedaemon" (5:78) is puzzling, since nothing elsewhere calls this legitimate king a tyrant; it is bound here as the same figure for lack of any textual signal of a second Charilaus, but the description does not obviously fit him.

entities.name: Minos
entities.body: The legendary king of Crete, credited with the laws still followed by its subject population and with Crete's naval empire; said to have died in Sicily. Cited again in Book 7 alongside Sesostris as an ancient founder of a warrior-versus-husbandmen class system.

entities.name: Ephialtes
entities.body: The Athenian statesman who, with Pericles, curtailed the power of the Areopagus.

entities.name: Pericles
entities.body: The Athenian statesman who, with Ephialtes, curtailed the power of the Areopagus and instituted payment for jury service.

entities.name: Zaleucus
entities.body: The lawgiver who gave laws to the Epizephyrian Locrians.

entities.name: Onomacritus
entities.body: A Locrian by birth trained in Crete, sometimes credited (on chronologically dubious authority) as the first legislator with any special skill, and placed by that same tradition as Thales's teacher.

entities.name: Philolaus the Corinthian
entities.body: A Theban legislator of the Corinthian Bacchiad family, who left Corinth for Thebes out of horror at his mother Halcyone's incestuous passion for him, and there gave the Thebans their "Laws of Adoption."

entities.name: Diocles
entities.body: The Olympic victor and lover of Philolaus, who left Corinth with him over the same scandal that drove Philolaus away. Original-en prints the OCR-mangled "Diodes"; both spellings are aliased and the error is left as printed.

entities.name: Halcyone
entities.body: Diocles's mother, whose incestuous passion for her son drove him and Philolaus from Corinth to Thebes.

entities.name: Draco
entities.body: The Athenian lawgiver, noted only for the severity of his penalties.

entities.name: Pittacus
entities.body: Elected leader (an aesymnetia, or elective tyranny) by the Mitylenaeans against exiles led by Antimenides and the poet Alcaeus; also cited as a lawgiver for a law doubling penalties for drunken violence.

entities.name: Antimenides
entities.body: One of the leaders of the exiles the Mitylenaeans elected Pittacus to oppose, named alongside the poet Alcaeus, his brother.

entities.name: Alcaeus
entities.body: The poet, one of the leaders of the exiles opposed to Pittacus, quoted denouncing his own city for making the low-born Pittacus tyrant.

entities.name: Androdamas of Rhegium
entities.body: Gave laws to the Chalcidians of Thrace, chiefly concerning homicide and heiresses.

entities.name: Phaleas of Chalcedon
entities.body: The first to propose that citizens of a state should have equal possessions; his equalization scheme and its limits occupy a long stretch of Book 2.

entities.name: Eubulus
entities.body: Talked Autophradates out of besieging Atarneus by pointing out the cost of the siege against the price of simply leaving.

entities.name: Autophradates
entities.body: The besieger of Atarneus whom Eubulus talked out of the siege.

entities.name: Diophantus
entities.body: Introduced the plan at Athens under which artisans engaged on public works are treated as public slaves.

entities.name: Jason
entities.body: Quoted for the remark that he "felt hungry when he was not a tyrant" -- unable to bear living as a private citizen.

entities.name: Euripides
entities.body: The tragedian, quoted on the special education of princes (Book 3), on living "according to one's fancy" as democratic license (Book 5), and elsewhere cited among those who scourged Decamnichus at Archelaus's court (Book 5).

entities.name: Lycophron
entities.body: The sophist, quoted for defining law as merely "a surety to one another of justice," a merely conventional guarantee rather than a maker of good citizens.

entities.name: Achilles
entities.body: The Homeric hero, cited complaining of Agamemnon's treating him "like some dishonoured stranger."

entities.name: Agamemnon
entities.body: The Homeric king, cited both for dishonouring Achilles and, elsewhere, for his prayer wishing for ten wise counsellors.

entities.name: Antisthenes
entities.body: The Cynic philosopher, whose fable of the lions and the hares -- "where are your claws?" -- is cited against demands for equality from the unequal.

entities.name: Heracles
entities.body: The legendary hero, said in myth to have been left behind by the Argonauts for fear he would overpower the rest of the crew -- an image for ostracism.

entities.name: Periander of Corinth
entities.body: The tyrant of Corinth, son of Cypselus, named in full at 5:67 as "the great master" of the arts of tyranny; identifiable elsewhere by the corn-field anecdote he shares with Thrasybulus of Miletus (3:54, 5:52) and by the Cypselid dynasty's reign lengths (5:75, 5:76, forty-four years, ending in 5:76's note that he was "a great soldier"). A different, unrelated Periander -- the tyrant of Ambracia -- is named in full elsewhere in Book 5.

entities.name: Thrasybulus of Miletus
entities.body: The tyrant of Miletus who received, via a herald, Periander of Corinth's wordless advice to cut down the tallest ears of corn -- meaning the leading citizens. A different, unrelated Thrasybulus -- Hiero's brother and successor as tyrant of Syracuse -- appears later in Book 5.

entities.name: Dionysius I
entities.body: The tyrant of Syracuse, cited repeatedly across Books 1, 3, and 5: asking the Syracusans for a bodyguard as his first step to power (3:70), rising by denouncing the rich (5:19), installed by Hipparinus (5:21), the Locrian marriage connection blamed for ruining that city (5:29), grouped among demagogues-turned-tyrant (5:49), and taxing his subjects into poverty within five years (5:67). His son and successor, Dionysius II, is a different, explicitly "younger" Dionysius named later in Book 5.

entities.name: Phocylides
entities.body: The gnomic poet, quoted praying for a middling competence.

entities.name: Telecles the Milesian
entities.body: Cited for a constitution in which citizens deliberate by turns rather than as a single body.

entities.name: Lysander
entities.body: The Spartan, said to have attempted to overthrow the Spartan monarchy.

entities.name: Pausanias (Spartan king)
entities.body: A king of Sparta who attempted to overthrow the ephoralty (5:2) and whom the Lacedaemonians later accused of trying to seize personal power in the state (7:57, both places naming him explicitly as "king"). Two different, unrelated men also named Pausanias appear elsewhere in Book 5: the regent who commanded at Plataea, and Philip of Macedon's assassin.

entities.name: Gelo
entities.body: The tyrant of Syracuse whose rise followed a period of democratic disorder there; his and his brother Hiero's dynasty is cited as the longest-lasting Syracusan tyranny, and its fall into a tyranny "distributed" among the family is discussed alongside Dionysius II's fall.

entities.name: Cleomenes
entities.body: The Lacedaemonian king whose defeat of the Argives in the "Battle of the Seventh Day" forced Argos to admit some of its subject population to citizenship.

entities.name: Heracleodorus
entities.body: His accession to office at Oreum overthrew the oligarchy there and changed it into a constitutional, democratic government.

entities.name: Paches
entities.body: The Athenian who took Mitylene in the war that followed a dispute there about heiresses.

entities.name: Timophanes (Mitylene)
entities.body: A wealthy citizen of Mitylene whose two daughters, sought by Doxander for his own sons and refused, occasioned a revolution. A different, unrelated Timophanes -- the Corinthian general who seized a tyranny -- appears later in Book 5.

entities.name: Doxander
entities.body: Wanted Timophanes's daughters for his sons; rejected, he stirred up revolution and, as Athenian proxenus, drew in Athenian interference at Mitylene.

entities.name: Mnaseas
entities.body: The father of Mnason, on one side of the Phocian heiress dispute that began the Sacred War.

entities.name: Mnason
entities.body: The son of Mnaseas, on one side of the Phocian heiress dispute that began the Sacred War.

entities.name: Euthycrates
entities.body: The father of Onomarchus, on the other side of the Phocian heiress dispute that began the Sacred War.

entities.name: Onomarchus
entities.body: The son of Euthycrates, on the other side of the Phocian heiress dispute that began the Sacred War.

entities.name: Phoxus
entities.body: The tyrant of Chalcis, killed by the people acting together with the notables, who then seized the government for themselves.

entities.name: Peisistratus
entities.body: The Athenian tyrant, who rose by leading a faction against the men of the plain; his rule and his sons' (the Peisistratidae) is cited repeatedly as an example of both tyranny's origins and its fall, and, in one anecdote, of a tyrant submitting to trial before the Areopagus.

entities.name: The Peisistratidae
entities.body: Peisistratus's family and dynasty at Athens, whose downfall -- provoked by the insult to Harmodius's sister -- and whose building projects (the temple of Olympian Zeus) are both cited.

entities.name: Theagenes
entities.body: The tyrant of Megara, who won popular favour by slaughtering the cattle of the wealthy.

entities.name: Daphnaeus
entities.body: One of the rich men whose denunciation by Dionysius I won him the people's confidence on his way to tyranny.

entities.name: Lygdamis
entities.body: A member of the oligarchy at Naxos who championed the oppressed people and afterward became tyrant himself.

entities.name: The Basilidae
entities.body: The family that ruled Erythrae well but was eventually deposed for the narrowness of its oligarchy.

entities.name: Charicles
entities.body: Led the dominant faction among the Thirty at Athens, an example of a demagogue operating within a small oligarchy.

entities.name: Phrynichus
entities.body: Led the dominant faction among the Four Hundred at Athens, an example of a demagogue operating within a small oligarchy.

entities.name: Simos
entities.body: Held the government at Larissa along with the Aleuadae family.

entities.name: The Aleuadae
entities.body: The ruling family of Larissa, who held the government there alongside Simos.

entities.name: Iphiades
entities.body: Associated with the political clubs that held power at Abydos.

entities.name: Cleotimus
entities.body: Introduced Chalcidian colonists at Amphipolis and then stirred them up against the rich.

entities.name: Hipparinus
entities.body: Installed Dionysius I as tyrant at Syracuse.

entities.name: Chares
entities.body: A political intermediary whose negotiation at Aegina became the occasion for an attempt to revolutionize the state there -- almost certainly the well-known Athenian general and mercenary commander, though the text gives no epithet to confirm it. A different, unrelated "Chares of Paros," an agricultural writer, is named in full in Book 1.

entities.name: Timophanes (Corinth)
entities.body: The Corinthian general who, given command of mercenaries, made himself tyrant -- the brother the celebrated liberator Timoleon later killed for it, though Aristotle does not name Timoleon here. A different, unrelated Timophanes -- an ordinary wealthy citizen of Mitylene -- appears earlier in Book 5.

entities.name: Diagoras
entities.body: Overturned the oligarchy of the knights at Eretria after being wronged in a marriage dispute.

entities.name: Eurytion
entities.body: Punished at Heraclea on a charge of adultery in a judgment executed in a spirit of party rather than justice, provoking revolution.

entities.name: Archias
entities.body: Punished at Thebes on a charge of adultery in a judgment executed in a spirit of party rather than justice, provoking revolution.

entities.name: The Partheniae
entities.body: The illegitimate sons of the Spartan peers, who attempted a revolution at Sparta and, once detected, were sent away to colonize Tarentum.

entities.name: Cinadon
entities.body: A brave man excluded from Sparta's honours, who conspired against the Spartans under Agesilaus.

entities.name: Agesilaus
entities.body: The Spartan king under whom Cinadon conspired against the Spartans.

entities.name: Tyrtaeus
entities.body: The poet whose "Good Order" is cited as evidence that citizens ruined by the Messenian War wanted a redistribution of land.

entities.name: Pausanias (the regent)
entities.body: Named as "general in the Persian War," cited as an example of an individual great enough to want to rule alone. Two different, unrelated men also named Pausanias appear elsewhere in Book 5: a Spartan king, and Philip of Macedon's assassin.

entities.name: Hanno
entities.body: A Carthaginian, cited alongside Pausanias as an example of an individual great enough to want to rule alone.

entities.name: Codrus
entities.body: Cited as a king who prevented his state from being enslaved in war, an example of royalty earned by benefiting one's people.

entities.name: Cyrus
entities.body: Cyrus the Great, cited as a king who gave his country freedom (5:50), and again as an example of a general who successfully attacked a monarch he despised -- his grandfather Astyages, whose power he judged worn out by soft living (5:59).

entities.name: Pheidon
entities.body: A king of Argos who became a tyrant, cited among rulers who extended hereditary power into outright tyranny. A different, unrelated Pheidon -- an ancient legislator -- is named in full ("Pheidon the Corinthian") in Book 2.

entities.name: Phalaris
entities.body: The tyrant of Acragas, cited as an example of a tyrant who rose from holding a great office rather than from being a demagogue.

entities.name: Panaetius
entities.body: Rose from demagogue to tyrant at Leontini; later cited again as an example of an oligarchy that changed directly into a tyranny.

entities.name: Cypselus
entities.body: The tyrant of Corinth and father of Periander, who rose as a demagogue, ruled without ever needing a bodyguard, and founded the Cypselid dynasty (thirty years' reign, then Periander's forty-four); his family's costly public offerings are cited as a device for keeping subjects poor and occupied.

entities.name: Harmodius
entities.body: The public dishonour of his sister, and the insult to himself, provoked the attack on the Peisistratidae that he and Aristogeiton carried out.

entities.name: Aristogeiton
entities.body: Joined Harmodius in the attack on the Peisistratidae, for Harmodius's sake.

entities.name: Periander of Ambracia
entities.body: The tyrant of Ambracia, expelled by the people acting with conspirators (5:15) and named in full ("Periander, the tyrant of Ambracia") as the target of a conspiracy provoked by an obscene question he asked a favourite youth (5:54). A different, unrelated Periander -- the tyrant of Corinth -- is Book 5's other, far more frequently cited Periander.

entities.name: Philip
entities.body: Philip II of Macedon, attacked by his own guard Pausanias after being permitted to suffer an insult from Attalus and his friends.

entities.name: Pausanias (assassin of Philip)
entities.body: Attacked Philip of Macedon after being permitted to suffer an insult from Attalus and his friends -- the historical assassin of Philip II, identified here by the surrounding narrative rather than an epithet. Two different, unrelated men also named Pausanias appear elsewhere in Book 5: a Spartan king, and the regent who commanded at Plataea.

entities.name: Attalus
entities.body: Insulted Pausanias, with the friends who joined him, provoking the attack on Philip of Macedon.

entities.name: Amyntas the Little
entities.body: Attacked by Derdas after boasting of having enjoyed Derdas's youth. A different, unrelated Amyntas -- Archelaus's own son -- is named later in the same passage.

entities.name: Derdas
entities.body: Attacked Amyntas the Little after being boasted of.

entities.name: Evagoras
entities.body: The king of Cyprus, slain by a eunuch avenging the eunuch's wife, whom Evagoras's own son had carried off.

entities.name: Crataeus
entities.body: Attacked and killed Archelaus, ostensibly over a broken marriage promise involving Archelaus's daughters, though Aristotle judges the real cause was Crataeus's disgust at their intimate connection.

entities.name: Archelaus
entities.body: The Macedonian king killed by Crataeus; the subject of several further conspiracies recounted in Book 5 (Hellanocrates, Decamnichus) arising from broken promises and personal insults.

entities.name: Sirrhas
entities.body: The enemy Archelaus was fighting when he married his elder daughter to the king of Elymaea for military support.

entities.name: Arrhibaeus
entities.body: Named alongside Sirrhas as an enemy Archelaus was fighting when he married his elder daughter to the king of Elymaea for military support.

entities.name: Amyntas (son of Archelaus)
entities.body: Archelaus's own son, married to Archelaus's younger daughter in hope of avoiding a quarrel with the son of Cleopatra. A different, unrelated Amyntas the Little is named earlier in the same passage.

entities.name: Cleopatra
entities.body: A Macedonian royal woman, mother of the son Archelaus hoped to keep from quarrelling with his own son Amyntas -- not the later, far better-known queen of Egypt.

entities.name: Hellanocrates of Larissa
entities.body: Archelaus's lover, who conspired against him after Archelaus failed to keep his promise of restoring him to his own country.

entities.name: Parrhon
entities.body: Killed Cotys with Heracleides of Aenos to avenge their father.

entities.name: Heracleides of Aenos
entities.body: Killed Cotys with Parrhon to avenge their father.

entities.name: Cotys
entities.body: The Thracian king killed by Parrhon and Heracleides of Aenos in revenge for their father, and mutilated Adamas as a child, provoking Adamas's own later revolt.

entities.name: Adamas
entities.body: Revolted from Cotys in revenge for being mutilated by him as a child.

entities.name: Megacles
entities.body: Attacked and killed the Penthalidae at Mitylene with his friends, after they had gone about the city assaulting people with clubs.

entities.name: The Penthalidae
entities.body: A ruling clan at Mitylene, killed by Megacles and his friends after going about assaulting people with clubs.

entities.name: Smerdis
entities.body: Beaten and torn from his wife by Penthilus, whom he later killed in revenge.

entities.name: Penthilus
entities.body: Beat Smerdis and tore him from his wife, and was later killed by him in revenge.

entities.name: Decamnichus
entities.body: Led the assassins in the conspiracy against Archelaus, enraged after Archelaus handed him over to Euripides to be scourged for a remark about the poet's bad breath.

entities.name: Artapanes
entities.body: Conspired against and killed Xerxes, fearing he would be blamed for hanging Darius without orders.

entities.name: Xerxes
entities.body: The Persian king, killed by Artapanes; also cited among rulers whose empires the Persian king (an earlier, unnamed reference) crushed rebellious former subjects.

entities.name: Darius
entities.body: Hanged, apparently on Artapanes's own initiative rather than Xerxes's orders -- probably Xerxes's own son of this name, distinct from Darius I "the Great."

entities.name: Sardanapalus
entities.body: The legendary Assyrian king, slain by a courtier who saw him carding wool among his women -- an example of contempt as a motive for conspiracy. Named only in modern-en; original-en's text is corrupted at this point and never supplies the name (see the package README).

entities.name: Dion
entities.body: Attacked and expelled his own relative Dionysius II out of contempt for his drunkenness, landing with only a small force on the principle that even a quick death would be an honourable risk.

entities.name: Dionysius II
entities.body: Dionysius I's son and successor as tyrant of Syracuse, explicitly called "the younger Dionysius," attacked out of contempt and then expelled by his own relative Dion.

entities.name: Astyages
entities.body: Cyrus's grandfather and the Median king Cyrus overthrew, his power judged worn out by an effeminate life.

entities.name: Seuthes
entities.body: A Thracian who conspired against Amadocus, the ruler whose general he was.

entities.name: Amadocus
entities.body: The Thracian ruler against whom his own general Seuthes conspired.

entities.name: Mithridates
entities.body: Conspired against Ariobarzanes out of a mix of contempt and love of gain.

entities.name: Ariobarzanes
entities.body: The ruler against whom his own subordinate Mithridates conspired.

entities.name: Theopompus
entities.body: The Spartan king who further limited royal power (chiefly by establishing the Ephoralty), reasoning that a reduced but more durable kingship was a better inheritance for his sons than a greater but less secure one.

entities.name: Hiero
entities.body: Gelo's brother and successor as tyrant of Syracuse, whose spies and informers are cited as a model of tyrannical surveillance; succeeded in turn by his own brother Thrasybulus.

entities.name: Thrasybulus (Syracuse)
entities.body: Hiero's brother, who flattered Gelo's son into excess in order to rule through him, provoking the family conspiracy that ended the dynasty (5:63); he later succeeded Hiero as tyrant in his own right, only to be driven out within eleven months (5:76). A different, unrelated Thrasybulus of Miletus is Book 5's other, far more frequently cited Thrasybulus.

entities.name: Myron
entities.body: The tyrant of Sicyon whose rule gave way to that of Cleisthenes of Sicyon.

entities.name: Cleisthenes of Sicyon
entities.body: The Orthagorid tyrant of Sicyon, respected for his military ability and said to have crowned the judge who ruled against him in the games. His rule followed Myron's (5:78) within the century-long Orthagorid tyranny (5:74). A different, unrelated Cleisthenes -- his own grandson, the Athenian democratic reformer -- appears in Books 3 and 6.

entities.name: Antileon
entities.body: His tyranny at Chalcis is cited as an example of a tyranny changing into an oligarchy.

entities.name: Cleander
entities.body: His tyranny at Gela is cited as an example of an oligarchy changing into a tyranny.

entities.name: Anaxilaus
entities.body: His tyranny at Rhegium is cited as an example of an oligarchy changing into a tyranny.

entities.name: Orthagoras
entities.body: Founder of the century-long Orthagorid tyranny at Sicyon, the longest-lasting of all -- attributed to the family's moderation and general observance of the laws.

entities.name: The Cypselidae
entities.body: The tyrant dynasty of Corinth founded by Cypselus, lasting seventy-three and a half years across Cypselus, Periander, and Psammetichus.

entities.name: Psammetichus
entities.body: Son of Gordius, the third and last of the Cypselid tyrants of Corinth, reigning three years after Periander.

entities.name: Oxylus
entities.body: Credited with an early law forbidding a man to borrow against a fixed portion of his property.

entities.name: Archilochus
entities.body: The poet, cited on the pleasures of leisure that follow the toil of war.

entities.name: Hippocrates
entities.body: The physician, cited as an example of a kind of "greatness" -- excellence in one's function -- that has nothing to do with physical size.

entities.name: Stentor
entities.body: The Homeric herald proverbial for a loud voice, invoked as a comparison for what statesmen wanting only more citizens would need.

entities.name: Sesostris
entities.body: The legendary Egyptian king credited with founding the warrior-versus-husbandmen class system later found in Egypt and Crete.

entities.name: Italus
entities.body: The legendary king of Oenotria after whom Italy is said to be named; credited with converting the Oenotrians from shepherds to husbandmen and founding their common meals.

entities.name: Scylax
entities.body: Cited for his claim that Indian kings hold no marked superiority over their subjects.

entities.name: Thibron
entities.body: Among the writers on the Spartan constitution who praised its legislator for the power hard training won the Lacedaemonians.

entities.name: Theodorus
entities.body: The tragic actor, who would not let any other actor -- however minor -- perform before him, since audiences grow fond of the first voice they hear.

entities.name: Odysseus
entities.body: The Homeric hero, quoted on the pleasure of a banquet with music.

entities.name: Musaeus
entities.body: The legendary poet, quoted on song as one of the pleasantest things.

entities.name: Olympus
entities.body: A musician (or composer) whose melodies are cited as proof that music can inspire real enthusiasm and moral feeling.

entities.name: Pauson
entities.body: A painter whose work young men should not be encouraged to look at, contrasted unfavourably with Polygnotus.

entities.name: Polygnotus
entities.body: A painter praised for expressing moral character in his work, contrasted favourably with Pauson.

entities.name: Archytas
entities.body: Credited with inventing the child's rattle -- a toy for the infant mind, as musical education is a toy for children of a larger growth.

entities.name: Philoxenus
entities.body: A dithyrambic poet who, having tried to compose his Tales in the Dorian mode, found it impossible and fell back into the more suitable Phrygian.

entities.name: Thrasippus
entities.body: Dedicated a tablet commemorating his sponsorship of a chorus for Ecphantides, cited as evidence of the flute's popularity at Athens.

entities.name: Ecphantides
entities.body: The Old Comedy poet for whom Thrasippus furnished a chorus.

entities.name: Athene
entities.body: The goddess, said in myth to have invented the flute and then thrown it away, on the reasoning (Aristotle's own gloss) that flute-playing contributes nothing to the mind.
